approved: Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Jobs for Families Child Care Package) Bill 2016
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a new Child Care Subsidy and an Additional Child Care Subsidy to replace existing payments.

The new system would set eligibility rules and payment calculations, with the Additional Child Care Subsidy targeting vulnerable families such as those at risk of abuse or experiencing financial hardship.
The main changes would start in July 2018, while some amendments would begin on Royal Assent or from July 2017.
Introduces a new Child Care Subsidy and an Additional Child Care Subsidy.
Replaces the current Child Care Benefit and Child Care Rebate.
Establishes eligibility criteria and payment calculation processes.
Provides targeted support for disadvantaged or vulnerable families.
Closes enrolment advance payments and allows their recovery from July 2017.
Sets out transition rules from the old system to the new one from July 2018.
Families using child care, approved child care providers, and the Department of Social Services.

Sarah Hanson-Young I would like to refer interested senators to the Greens amendment on sheet 8109. This is in relation to lifting the number of hours in the safety net from 12 to 15. We have heard consistently from the sector, the childcare providers as well as education experts, that we should not be reducing the number of hours available for vulnerable and low-income families, and children in particular. This safety net can only operate as a safety net if it indeed gives children the protection that ensures they are able to succeed and benefit from the care and educational experience and opportunities they are given. This amendment goes to put into practice the idea that two days of child care and early childhood education would be available to vulnerable and low-income families. These are families who do not meet the activity test for a variety of reasons. This might include single parent families or families where one parent is at home and not able to work or is transitioning through different work arrangements. I heard the minister in his speech just now trying to argue that 12 hours of care is sufficient, but it is just not. Currently, these families have access to 24 hours of care a week. The current bill, unless this amendment is accepted, would halve that access for some of the most vulnerable and disadvantaged families we have. I would like to keep it at 24 hours per week, but I am being realistic here tonight that there has been a lot of consultation and compromise from people on many fronts to accept that 15 hours would be the bare minimum. The rationale for 15 hours is that it is neatly split between two days, at 7½ hours per day, which ensures children can get the maximum benefit from that care. We also know that from a provider's perspective—that is, each individual childcare centre—that it is more realistic for them to be able to operate a system where they can provide 7½ hours of care each day, or 15 hours of care split evenly over two days. The majority voted to pass the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5696) in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [third time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). But since new amendments were agreed to in the Senate, the bill won't be made into law yet. First it needs to go back to the House of Representatives where they'll decide to either: (1) agree with the amendments so the bill will become law; or (2) disagree with the amendments and ask the Senate if they insist on them (if the Senate does, the bill can't become law because both levels of Parliament must agree on the wording of a bill). ### What is this bill? According to the bill's digest, if passed the bill will introduce *a new child care fee assistance payment, the Child Care Subsidy (CCS), replacing two current payments: [Child Care Benefit](https://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-benefit) (CCB) and [Child Care Rebate](https://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-rebate) (CCR).* It will also introduce a new supplementary payment, called the Additional Child Care Subsidy (ACCS), which will: > *additional financial assistance for children at risk of abuse or neglect, families experiencing temporary financial hardship, families transitioning to work from income support, grandparent carers on income support, and low income families in certain circumstances. The ACCS partly replaces a number of current payments including Special Child Care Benefit, Grandparent Child Care Benefit and the Jobs, Education and Training Child Care Fee Assistance payment.*

The bill funds the Jobs for Families Child Care Package by reforming family payments, including increasing Family Tax Benefit Part A fortnightly rates by $10.08 per child, phasing out end-of-year supplements, and restructuring Family Tax Benefit Part B from 2017-18. It also aligns youth allowance rates for under-18s and extends some FTB B eligibility for single parents and grandparent carers.

The bill introduces the Jobs for Families Child Care Package, investing around $40 billion over four years, including a new means-tested childcare subsidy with rates from 85% for low-income families down to 20% for high-income families, an activity test linking subsidised hours to work or study, and an additional subsidy for disadvantaged children. The package also includes strengthened compliance measures and is contingent on passing savings from the Family Payments Reform Bill.

The speaker argued the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Jobs for Families Child Care Package) Bill 2016 is a lost opportunity that would leave one in three families worse off, cut minimum child care hours from 24 to 12, and disadvantage vulnerable children through a flawed activity test. They cited research showing a 16-fold return on investment in early childhood education and listed organisations opposing the bill, including the Australian Childcare Alliance and the Brotherhood of St Laurence.

The speaker opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Jobs for Families Child Care Package) Bill, arguing it cuts funding for low-income, single-parent, and Indigenous families. They cited ANU research that 330,000 families would be worse off, with 71,000 families earning under $65,000 specifically affected.

The speaker argued that the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Jobs for Families Child Care Package) Bill 2016 fails rural and regional Australia because it is designed for centre-based care and does not address communities without childcare centres, noting that the government rejected amendments to test the reforms' effectiveness. The speaker also called on the Regional Ministerial Task Force to develop a coherent regional policy, citing the need for long-term, needs-based funding rather than short-term grants.

The speaker argued that the current childcare system makes it cheaper for parents to stay home on welfare than to work, citing a constituent paying $1,200 a week for care during school holidays after hitting the $7,500 cap. They supported the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Jobs for Families Child Care Package) Bill to make childcare affordable and incentivise workforce participation.

Labor did not oppose amendments cutting subsidies for high-income families but argued the package would halve early childhood education access for vulnerable children from 24 to 12 hours per week, criticizing a Senate deal with Nick Xenophon and One Nation.
